text: Peter George Doyle (June 1843 – April 19, 1907) was an Irish-born American transit worker who served as an intimate companion to Walt Whitman from approximately 1865 to 1876, and to some extent until Whitman's death in 1892. Doyle was born in early June 1843 in Ireland to Peter George Doyle, a blacksmith, and Catherine Nash Doyle, the sixth of nine children; he was baptized on June 16, 1843, in Limerick. The family moved to Alexandria, Virginia, in 1853, arriving in Baltimore on May 10 before settling there. Doyle received little formal education and stood about 5 feet 8 inches tall. His niece described him as "a homosexual." Between 1856 and 1859, the Doyles relocated to Richmond, Virginia, where Peter Sr. worked at the Tredegar Iron Works. When the American Civil War began, Doyle enlisted in the Confederate States Army on April 25, 1861, fought in several battles including the Battle of Antietam (where he was wounded), and was discharged on November 7, 1862. He likely re-joined the army in 1863 before deserting and fleeing north, where he was briefly imprisoned near Old Capitol Prison in April 1863 and released on May 11. He then worked at the Washington Navy Yard in Washington, D.C., until 1865. After the war, he lived in Washington, D.C., and worked as a streetcar conductor for the Washington and Georgetown Railroad Company. Doyle was an eyewitness to the assassination of Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, and Whitman later referenced his account. Doyle first met Whitman in 1865 on a "cold, stormy night" when Whitman was the only passenger on Doyle’s streetcar; the two became close friends, corresponding regularly and meeting frequently. Whitman often rode Doyle’s streetcar, went on hikes together, and wrote many letters, addressing Doyle as "boy" or "son," while Doyle signed his name "Pete the Great." Historian Martin G. Murray suggested that Doyle may have influenced Whitman’s poem "O Captain! My Captain!" by prompting a shift to a more conventional form, and that the hero in "Come Up From the Fields, Father" is named "Pete," with Murray arguing Doyle may have inspired some poems in Drum-Taps. In May 1870, the two traveled briefly to New York City to see the opera Poliuto; Whitman abbreviated Doyle’s name in his diary as "16.4" (P being the 16th letter, D the fourth). Whitman may have begun to suspect he loved Doyle, though Doyle did not reciprocate fully, as he was supporting his mother; by the end of 1870, Whitman was more confident in their bond. In 1872 or 1873, Doyle began working as a braker on the Pennsylvania Railroad. After Whitman suffered a stroke in 1873, Doyle helped nurse him. Doyle grew increasingly dissatisfied with his job and continued visiting Whitman even after he moved to Camden, New Jersey, in 1874. After 1876, their correspondence and visits declined significantly. In 1880, Doyle met Richard Maurice Bucke, a promoter and early biographer of Whitman. After 1885, he moved permanently to Philadelphia, where he was a member of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks and joined the United Confederate Veterans. The last known contact between Doyle and Whitman may have been in 1889, though they likely met at least once afterward. Whitman left Doyle his watch, and Doyle visited Whitman’s body after his death in 1892, though he was nearly denied entry to the funeral. Doyle was also friends with Horace Traubel and his wife Anne Traubel, as well as Gustave Percival Wiksell. Whitman’s letters to Doyle were published in 1895 as *Calamus, A Series of Letters Written During the Years 1868–1880 by Walt Whitman To A Young Friend (Peter Doyle)*, which is generally recognized as a collection of love letters and received mixed reviews. After Whitman’s death, Doyle kept a coat that Whitman had worn, describing it as "like Aladdin's lamp." For the rest of his life, Doyle was regarded as a celebrity by Whitman’s friends and followers. A portrait of Doyle and Whitman, taken around 1865 by M. P. Rice, is the earliest known portrait of Whitman with someone else. John Burroughs paraphrased Thomas Gray’s "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" to describe Doyle as "a mute inglorious Whitman." Doyle is considered the most likely candidate for Whitman’s lifelong love, and biographer Justin Kaplan wrote in 1980 that Whitman extended himself with Doyle more than with any other man, at greater risk to his psychological well-being. Their relationship is often described as a "romantic friendship," though its exact nature remains unknown. Doyle died on April 19, 1907, in Philadelphia from uremia and is buried in the Congressional Cemetery in Washington, D.C.
